newsitem.title: JAPAN: MOF says believes SESC likely to probe brokerages.
newsitem.headline: MOF says believes SESC likely to probe brokerages.

text.p: Japan's Finance Minister Hiroshi Mitsuzuka said on Friday he believes the Securities and Exchange Surveillance Commission (SESC) will likely probe the three other "Big Four" brokerages which have been reported to have had links with the "sokaiya" corporate racketeer cited in the case of Nomura Securities Co Ltd.
"It's hard to believe the authorities will sit by after such reports. It's common sense for them to conduct an appropriate investigation," he said.
He added: "I think the SESC and the Finance Ministry will move to see whether there are links as reported."
But Mitsuzuka did not clarify whether any formal investigation was planned.

Corporate clients linked to a sokaiya named in a recent scandal involving suspected illegal deals at Nomura also have accounts at the rest of Japan's "Big Four" brokerages, a newspaper reported on Friday.

The Mainichi Shimbun report said the SESC, Japan's securities watchdog, found that the corporate clients opened accounts with Daiwa Securities Co Ltd, Nikko Securities Co Ltd and Yamaichi Securities Co Ltd at the same time as they did at Nomura.
Separately, Mitsuzuka said the Finance Ministry had decided to cut the rate on deposits at its Trust Fund Bureau by 0.1 percentage point to 2.8 percent.
The rate will go into effect from March 19.
The rate is paid on deposits made at the bureau by public pension and postal savings funds.

The financial daily Nihon Keizai Shimbun had reported on Friday that Japan's Health and Welfare Ministry had agreed to a cut in the rate on its deposits at the Trust Fund Bureau early next week by 0.1 percentage point to 2.8 percent.

Asked about Japan's GDP figures released on Thursday, Mitsuzuka said they showed the firmness of the economic recovery, adding that Japan was likely to achieve the government's target of 2.5 percent growth for this fiscal year ending on March 31.

He also said growth would slow temporarily in the first half of the next fiscal year starting April 1 due to fiscal tightening measures, but added it would recover in the latter half and move towards achieving the government's 1.9 growth target for the year.
The government plans to raise the consumption tax to five percent from three percent and also end special tax cuts from April 1.
